title: Probability Distributions Computed by Autoregressive Transformers
claim: Autoregression can raise expressivity over classifiers in the Boolean setting, and making models probabilistic breaks equivalences that otherwise hold.
layout: 2 panels split by vertical line, bottom-to-top inclusion arrows, labeled theorem links
description: A figure with two panels separated by a thin vertical gray line. Each panel is a small diagram of language classes arranged in two columns, with black arrows between them. In the left panel (Boolean semiring), the two columns are the classifier and the autoregressor. Each column has a bottom node, 'leftmost UHATs = fixed-precision SMATs = TL[P]', with an upward arrow to a top node, 'rightmost UHATs = LTL'. A double-headed arrow labeled 'Thm. 5.6' joins the top nodes. A single right arrow labeled 'Prop. 5.8' joins the bottom nodes. The right panel (real semiring) has the same layout, but the links between columns are slashed arrows labeled 'Cor. 5.4', meaning incomparable. The top right node also has an upward arrow, labeled 'Prop. 5.5', to 'cfNFAs'. Reference labels are dark blue. The text is black. The eye goes first to the central rows of class names.
caption: In the Boolean semiring, equivalences from the literature (Yang et al., 2024; Jerad et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025) carry over from classifiers to autoregressors; however, sometimes autoregressors are more expressive than classifiers. In the real semiring, LTL and counter-free DFAs and NFAs become less expressive than counter-free NFAs, and rightmost UHATs are only as expressive as the former. Key: strict inclusion, equivalence.̸ = incomparable.
abstract: Most expressivity results for transformers treat them as language recognizers -- devices that accept or reject strings -- rather than as they are used in practice: as language models that generate strings autoregressively and probabilistically. We characterize the probability distributions that transformer language models can express. We show that making transformer language recognizers autoregressive can sometimes increase their expressivity, and that making them probabilistic can break equivalences that hold in the non-probabilistic case. Our overall contribution is to tease apart what functions transformers are capable of expressing in their most common use case as language models.
